- When sentiment is consistently positive (≥0.67) over recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast slightly, especially after recent spikes.
- When sentiment is negative (≤0.33) or volatile, model often underestimates; adjust upward, particularly if price has recently fallen sharply.
- Model frequently overreacts to short-term sentiment spikes — forecast overshoots by 2–5% after sentiment jumps to 1.00; apply dampening factor (e.g., cap forecast at 10% above recent mean).
- If true outcome shows strong mean reversion (e.g., 3–5 consecutive days below 65–70), model tends to lag — adjust forecast downward by 1–3% for next 3–5 days.
- For 30-day horizon, model often fails to capture long-term downward trends; if sentiment is negative over 5+ days, reduce forecast by 2–4% per day until sentiment stabilizes.
- If sentiment history shows alternating highs/lows (e.g., 0.67, 0.33, 0.67), model tends to oscillate — smooth forecast by averaging last 3–5 values before applying sentiment-weighted adjustment.
- When model forecast is >75% of recent 10-day average, reduce by 5–10% if sentiment is neutral or negative; if sentiment is positive, allow slight overshoot but cap at 80% of recent high.
